about: POL1, The Modern State and its Alternatives, is the first-year introduction to politics in the Cambridge Human, Social, and Political Sciences Tripos, recommended for the Politics and International Relations track. It is taught through set texts read for their arguments: in 2024-25, eight two-lecture blocks in Michaelmas (Hobbes, Weber, Constant, Hayek, Arendt, The Federalist and Brutus, Tocqueville, Schumpeter) and eight in Lent (Mair, Acemoglu and Robinson, Castoriadis and Vardoulakis, Marx and Engels, Gandhi, Schmitt, Fanon, MacKinnon), with supervisions in each term. The 2024-25 paper guide describes assessment as one three-hour written exam in three sections, answering three questions drawn from at least two sections, with no formally assessed coursework. Set texts can change between years, so check your current paper guide.
topics: Hobbes and the problem of order (Leviathan)
Arendt and the human condition in the nuclear age
The American federal republic: The Federalist and Brutus
Tocqueville: democratic society and its adaptability
Schumpeter: democracy as a competitive struggle for power
Representative democracy in question: Mair, Acemoglu and Robinson, Castoriadis and Vardoulakis
Marx and Engels: The Communist Manifesto
Gandhi: Hind Swaraj and the sovereign soul
Schmitt: The Concept of the Political
Empire and gender: Fanon and MacKinnon

Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) published Leviathan in London in 1651, after the English Civil War, having written it largely in exile in Paris. The set reading is Parts I ("Of Man") and II ("Of Commonwealth"). His question is how a stable political order is possible among people who disagree deeply, especially about religion.

The natural condition of mankind (chapter 13)
- Humans are roughly equal: even the weakest can kill the strongest by cunning or alliance.
- Equality of ability breeds equality of hope, so people compete for the same things.
- Three principal causes of quarrel: competition (for gain), diffidence (distrust, seeking safety) and glory (reputation).
- Without a common power to keep them all in awe, people are in a condition of war "of every man against every man". War means a known disposition to fight, not constant battle.
- There is no industry, culture or society, and life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short". There is no justice or property, because there is no common power to define them.

Right and law of nature (chapters 14–15)
- The right of nature is the liberty each person has to use their own power to preserve their life, by any means they judge fit; in the natural condition this extends to a right to all things.
- A law of nature is a rule, found by reason, forbidding a person to do what destroys their own life. The first is to seek peace and follow it, and, failing that, to defend ourselves by all means. The second is to lay down the right to all things, if others will do so too. The third is to keep covenants made: this is the origin of justice.
- Covenants in the natural condition are unreliable because nobody can be sure the other will perform: "covenants, without the sword, are but words" (chapter 17).

Authorisation and the sovereign (chapters 16–18)
- Each person covenants with every other to authorise one man or assembly to act in their name: the many become one person, the commonwealth, whose representative is the sovereign. Hobbes calls this the "great Leviathan", a "mortal god".
- Because subjects are authors of the sovereign's actions, the sovereign cannot injure them, cannot be lawfully punished by them, and is not a party to the covenant, so cannot breach it.
- Sovereignty must be undivided. It includes making law, judging controversies, war and peace, choosing officials and judging which doctrines may be taught. Divided sovereignty, as Hobbes thought had happened between king and Parliament, leads to civil war (chapter 29).
- A commonwealth can arise by institution (agreement) or acquisition (conquest). Covenants made from fear are still binding.

Liberty of subjects (chapter 21)
- Liberty means the absence of external impediments to motion, so it is consistent with fear and with necessity.
- Subjects' liberty lies in the "silence of the law": what the sovereign has not regulated.
- Some rights cannot be given up: a subject may resist being killed, wounded or imprisoned, and need not kill or accuse themselves.
- Obligation lasts only as long as the sovereign can protect: protection and obedience go together.

Key debates
- Is the sovereign too powerful? Hobbes replies that any power able to protect must be absolute, and that the alternative, civil war, is far worse.
- Is Hobbes a theorist of the modern state? His account of the commonwealth as an artificial person, distinct from both rulers and ruled, is often read as a founding statement of the impersonal state.
- Prisoners' dilemma readings model the state of nature as a collective action problem.

Exam tips: quote chapter references, distinguish the right of nature from the law of nature, and use chapter 21 to test how absolute sovereign power really is.

notes.h: Weber, 'The Profession and Vocation of Politics' (1919)
notes.body:
Max Weber (1864–1920) gave this lecture in Munich in January 1919, weeks after Germany's defeat and amid revolution. The lecture, usually translated as "Politics as a Vocation", asks what politics is, what kind of people now live by it, and what ethical demands it places on them.

The state and legitimacy
- Weber defines the state not by its ends (states pursue all sorts of goals) but by its means: physical force. The modern state is the human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.
- Politics means striving to share in power or to influence how it is distributed, between or within states.
- Rule needs inner justification. There are three pure types of legitimate domination:
  - traditional (the authority of the "eternal yesterday", custom)
  - charismatic (devotion to the extraordinary personal gifts of a leader)
  - legal (rational) (belief in the validity of rationally made rules and in competence defined by them)

Living for and living off politics
- Politics can be pursued as an occasional, part-time or full-time activity. People live "for" politics (finding meaning in it) or "off" it (as a source of income).
- Modern politics creates professional politicians alongside a trained, expert bureaucracy. Officials should administer impartially; politicians must take sides and personal responsibility.
- Mass democracy and party machines (Weber discusses the British caucus system and American party bosses) give rise to plebiscitary leaders who win followers through demagogy. The choice is between leadership democracy "with a machine" and leaderless rule by professional politicians without vocation.

Qualities of a politician
- Passion (devotion to a cause), a sense of responsibility, and a sense of proportion (judgement, the ability to keep distance from things and people).
- The besetting sin is vanity: pursuing power for its own sake or for show.

The two ethics
- Ethic of conviction (often translated "ethic of ultimate ends"): act rightly and leave the outcome to God; responsibility for bad consequences lies with the world or others. Weber's example is the Sermon on the Mount, and the revolutionary syndicalist.
- Ethic of responsibility: one must answer for the foreseeable consequences of one's actions.
- Because politics works with the specific means of violence, good ends may require morally dubious means, and good intentions can produce evil outcomes. The world is ethically irrational.
- Weber does not simply dismiss conviction. He suggests a mature person who acts responsibly may reach a point where they say, with Luther, "Here I stand; I can do no other". At that point the two ethics are complementary.

Conclusions
- Politics is "a strong and slow boring of hard boards", needing both passion and judgement.
- Weber warns that the near future will be a "polar night of icy darkness" rather than a summer's bloom.

Connections in POL1
- Hobbes: both treat the state as defined by its control of force, but Weber stresses legitimacy and the dangers of bureaucracy and leaderless politics.
- Schumpeter: shares Weber's view of democracy as competition between leaders for mass support.

Exam tips: get the monopoly definition exactly right (successfully claims, legitimate, physical force, territory), explain the two ethics fairly, and ask whether Weber's ideal politician is attractive or dangerous.

Benjamin Constant (1767–1830), Swiss-born French liberal writer and politician, lived through the Revolution, the Terror and Napoleon. The set texts are his lecture "The Liberty of the Ancients Compared with that of the Moderns" (given at the Athénée Royal in Paris in 1819) and Principles of Politics Applicable to All Representative Governments (1815).

Two kinds of liberty
- Liberty of the ancients (e.g. Athens, Sparta, Rome): exercising sovereignty collectively and directly, deliberating in public on war and peace, voting laws, judging magistrates. It was compatible with the complete subjection of the individual to the community: private life, religion and opinion could be controlled.
- Liberty of the moderns: the peaceful enjoyment of private independence. Each person has the right to be subject only to the laws, to express opinions, choose an occupation, dispose of property, associate, worship and come and go, and to have some influence over government through representatives or petitions.

Why liberty changed
- Modern states are much larger, so each citizen's share of sovereignty is tiny and they cannot feel its importance.
- The abolition of slavery means citizens must work and have little leisure for constant politics.
- Commerce has replaced war as the main way of obtaining what one wants. Commerce gives individuals independence, makes them love it and makes property harder for governments to seize.

The danger of misapplying ancient liberty
- Constant blamed thinkers such as Rousseau and Mably, and the revolutionaries who followed them, for trying to impose ancient collective liberty on modern people. The result was the tyranny of the Terror, carried out in the name of liberty.
- In Principles of Politics, he argues that popular sovereignty is not unlimited. Some areas of life must lie beyond any authority, whether one, few or many: abstract sovereignty in the hands of the people can be as tyrannical as a monarch.

Representative government
- The representative system is the modern solution: like wealthy people who employ stewards to manage their estates, citizens entrust public affairs to representatives because they are busy with their own lives.
- But stewards must be watched. The danger of modern liberty is that, absorbed in private enjoyment, people give up their share of political power too easily, letting rulers take over.
- Political liberty is therefore the indispensable guarantee of individual liberty. Constant concludes that we must learn to combine the two, and that political participation also improves citizens morally.

Other themes from Principles of Politics
- Individual rights, a free press, independent courts and limits on arbitrary power.
- A constitutional monarch as a "neutral power" standing above the active powers to restore balance between them.

Connections in POL1
- Hobbes defines liberty as absence of impediments and leaves it to the silence of the law; Constant puts individual rights beyond sovereign reach.
- Tocqueville shares Constant's worry that private, commercial citizens will withdraw from public life.
- Mair's account of citizens withdrawing from party politics can be read as Constant's danger realised.

Exam tips: avoid treating Constant as simply anti-participation. His argument is that modern liberty needs political liberty to protect it, and that representation must be supervised by active citizens.

Friedrich Hayek (1899–1992), an Austrian economist then at the London School of Economics, published The Road to Serfdom in 1944 and dedicated it "to the socialists of all parties". His argument is that central economic planning, however well meant, leads towards totalitarianism. He wrote it in Britain during the war, arguing that the forces that produced Nazism in Germany were at work in British thinking too.

The abandoned road
- Liberalism and competitive markets had produced unprecedented freedom and prosperity. Impatience with their slower progress led intellectuals to embrace planning.
- Socialism promised a "new freedom" from want, but Hayek argues this confuses freedom with power or wealth.

Why planning threatens freedom
- Central planning means directing all economic activity according to a single plan. To do so, planners must rank all the different ends people pursue.
- But there is no complete ethical code on which everyone agrees. Democratic assemblies can agree on general principles but not on detailed plans, so they become frustrated and delegate power to experts or a strong leader.
- Economic control is not control of one sector of life. Because money is the means to all our ends, whoever controls the economy controls the means for all our ends, and so decides which ends are pursued.

Planning and the rule of law (chapter 6)
- The rule of law means government is bound by rules fixed and announced beforehand, so individuals can foresee how coercive power will be used and plan their own affairs.
- Planning requires discretionary decisions about particular people and cases, which formal rules cannot capture. It therefore erodes the rule of law. Formal equality before the law conflicts with deliberately pursuing substantive equality.

Why the worst get on top (chapter 10)
- To win support for a single plan, leaders must appeal to the least discriminating, most docile and gullible people and unite them against a common enemy.
- Those willing to do whatever the plan requires, without moral scruples, rise. Totalitarian features are not accidents but follow from the logic of planning.

What Hayek does not say
- He is not a pure laissez-faire thinker. He supports planning for competition (designing legal frameworks so that competition works), regulations such as limits on working hours and sanitary rules, and some state provision.
- He accepts that a minimum of food, shelter and clothing can be guaranteed to all, and insurance against common hazards such as sickness, as long as this does not replace the market.

Critical debates
- Critics argue that mixed economies and welfare states in post-war Western Europe did not lead to serfdom, so Hayek's "slippery slope" was not borne out empirically.
- Defenders answer that his target was comprehensive central planning, not social insurance.
- His view of democracy is instrumental: democracy is valuable as a safeguard of liberty, not in itself.

Connections in POL1
- Constant: both defend modern individual liberty against claims made in the name of the collective.
- Arendt and Schmitt offer very different accounts of what politics is; Acemoglu and Robinson link economic institutions to political ones.
- Marx and Engels provide the critique of capitalism that Hayek is resisting.

Exam tips: reconstruct the argument step by step (no agreed ranking of ends → delegation to planners → discretion replaces the rule of law → coercion), then test each step.

Hannah Arendt (1906–1975), a German-Jewish political thinker who fled Nazi Germany and settled in the United States, published The Human Condition in 1958. It followed The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951). The book asks "what we are doing" in the modern world.

The nuclear and space age
- The Prologue opens with the launch of the first artificial satellite (1957), which Arendt reads as a sign of a wish to escape the human condition itself, including our bond to the earth.
- She distinguishes the modern age, which began scientifically in the seventeenth century, from the modern world, which she says was born politically with the first atomic explosions. Science now gives humans the power to destroy organic life on earth and to act into nature, starting processes they cannot control.

The vita activa: three activities
- Labour: the activity that corresponds to the biological process of the body. Its products are consumed almost as soon as they are made; it is endless and repetitive. The human as animal laborans.
- Work: fabrication of a durable world of objects (tools, buildings, artworks) that outlasts its makers and gives human life stability. The human as homo faber, working by means and ends.
- Action: the only activity that goes on directly between people, without the medium of things. It corresponds to the human condition of plurality: we are all human, but no two of us are the same. Action takes place through speech and deeds, reveals who someone is, and depends on others seeing and hearing it.

Natality and power
- Natality: because each person is a new beginning, humans can begin something new. Action is the capacity to start unpredictable new processes.
- Power springs up between people when they act together and vanishes when they disperse. It is distinct from strength (individual) and force or violence (instruments).

Public and private
- Drawing on the Greek polis and household, Arendt separates the private realm of necessity (the household, where needs are met) from the public realm of freedom (where equals appear to each other).
- The modern rise of "the social" blurs this: housekeeping concerns, such as the economy, become the central business of politics, and behaviour replaces action. Society expects conformity.

The frailty of action
- Action is unpredictable (consequences go beyond what anyone intends) and irreversible (what is done cannot be undone).
- The remedies come from within action itself: the faculty of making and keeping promises, which creates islands of predictability, and the faculty of forgiving, which releases people from the consequences of what they have done.

Modern world alienation
- Modernity brought world alienation (loss of a shared, durable world) and earth alienation (the scientific viewpoint from outside the earth).
- The victory of labour: modern society is a society of jobholders, and automation threatens a society of labourers without labour, the worst possible outcome.

Connections in POL1
- Unlike Weber and Hobbes, Arendt separates power from violence.
- Against Hayek and Marx, she criticises making economic life the focus of politics.
- Castoriadis shares her admiration for Athenian democracy and her stress on creating something new.

Exam tips: define labour, work and action precisely, explain why action needs plurality, and connect the Prologue's nuclear and space-age themes to her worry about uncontrollable processes.

In 1787 the Philadelphia Convention proposed a new Constitution to replace the weak Articles of Confederation. During the ratification debate in New York, Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote 85 essays under the shared pen name "Publius": The Federalist. Opponents, the Anti-Federalists, replied; among the most important were the letters of "Brutus" (often attributed to Robert Yates, though this is uncertain).

Why a new constitution? (Federalist 1 and 22)
- Federalist 1 (Hamilton) frames the question: can societies establish good government by reflection and choice, or are they destined to depend on accident and force?
- Federalist 22 lists further defects of the Confederation, such as the lack of power to regulate commerce, the equal vote of large and small states and the absence of a national judiciary.

Faction and the extended republic (Federalist 10, Madison)
- A faction is a group of citizens, majority or minority, united by a common passion or interest adverse to the rights of other citizens or the permanent interests of the community.
- Its causes are "sown in the nature of man". The most common and durable source is the unequal distribution of property.
- Removing the causes would destroy liberty, so the aim is to control the effects.
- A pure democracy cannot cure majority faction. A republic, meaning government by representation, can: representatives may "refine and enlarge the public views".
- A large republic is better than a small one: "extend the sphere" and you take in a greater variety of interests, making it harder for a majority to form an oppressive faction. Federalist 14 defends the feasibility of a large republic.

The Constitution's structure (Federalist 37–39, 47–48, 51)
- Federalist 39: the government is "partly national, partly federal", a compound republic.
- Federalist 47–48: separation of powers (citing Montesquieu) does not require complete separation; written "parchment barriers" are not enough.
- Federalist 51: each branch needs the means and personal motives to resist encroachment. "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition." "If men were angels, no government would be necessary." Federalism and separation of powers give a "double security" to rights.

Representation (Federalist 57–58, 63)
- The House of Representatives is defended as close enough to the people; the Senate as providing stability and wisdom.
- Federalist 63 identifies the distinctive feature of American government as the total exclusion of the people in their collective capacity from any share in it: the people govern only through representatives.

The judiciary (Federalist 78, Hamilton)
- The judiciary is the "least dangerous" branch, having "neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment".
- Courts may declare laws contrary to the Constitution void, because the Constitution expresses the will of the people, which is superior to the legislature. This defends judicial review and life tenure.

Brutus's objections
- Brutus I: a free republic cannot exist over so large a territory (drawing on Montesquieu); the "necessary and proper" and taxing powers will lead to a consolidated national government swallowing the states.
- Representatives should resemble those they represent and share their sentiments. Too few representatives will be drawn mainly from elites and will not know or reflect the people.
- Brutus XI: the federal judiciary, interpreting the Constitution according to its "spirit" and unaccountable to anyone, will steadily extend federal power. Federalist 78 is often read as a reply to these concerns.

Exam tips: present the Federalist–Anti-Federalist exchange as a debate about what representation is (filter versus mirror) and whether a large republic can be free. Link to Tocqueville and Schumpeter.

Alexis de Tocqueville (1805–1859), a French aristocrat, travelled in the United States in 1831–32, officially to study prisons, with his friend Gustave de Beaumont. The two volumes of Democracy in America appeared in 1835 and 1840. The set reading is selected chapters from both.

Equality of conditions
- The "generating fact" of American society is equality of conditions: the absence of hereditary ranks, so that people regard each other as broadly equal in status.
- Tocqueville treats democracy as a social state as well as a form of government. He sees the advance of equality in Europe too as irresistible, almost providential. The question is not whether democracy will come, but whether it will be free or despotic.
- He writes to help France, which has had a democratic revolution without the habits and institutions that make democracy work.

Dangers of democracy
- Tyranny of the majority: the majority's power over both government and opinion can crush minorities and independent thought. In America the danger lay less in physical oppression than in pressure on the mind: Tocqueville claimed he knew no country with less independence of mind and real freedom of discussion.
- Individualism: a calm, considered feeling that leads each citizen to withdraw into a small circle of family and friends, leaving the wider society to itself. It differs from egoism, which is a passionate self-love. Equality isolates people, because no hereditary ties bind them.
- Soft despotism (Volume 2): an immense, tutelary power that takes charge of people's welfare and pleasures, keeping them in perpetual childhood. It does not tyrannise, but degrades, gradually relieving citizens of the trouble of thinking and acting for themselves.
- Materialism, restlessness and love of well-being can make citizens trade freedom for order.

Remedies and sources of strength
- Local self-government, especially the New England township, which teaches citizens to take an interest in public affairs.
- Civil and political associations: the "art of association" lets weak, equal individuals combine to achieve what aristocrats once did alone.
- A free press, the jury (a free school that teaches citizens to judge) and the legal profession, which acts as a counterweight to democratic passions.
- Religion, which moderates materialism and sets limits to what people think they may do, kept separate from the state.
- "Self-interest properly understood": Americans explain their public-spiritedness as enlightened self-interest.
- Mores (habits of the heart and mind) matter more than laws or physical circumstances in sustaining democracy.

Democratic adaptability
- Democratic government makes more mistakes than aristocratic government and is often clumsy and short-sighted. But its laws generally aim at the good of the greatest number, and its errors can be corrected.
- American advantages include the ability to make mistakes that can be repaired. This idea of democracy's self-correcting capacity is central to the POL1 lecture theme.

Connections in POL1
- Constant: both fear that private, commercial citizens will withdraw from politics.
- The Federalist: Tocqueville admired American federalism but feared the majority that Madison sought to filter.
- Mair: declining participation and party membership look like individualism realised.
- Arendt: both admire associational and participatory life.

Exam tips: distinguish political institutions from social conditions, explain how associations counter individualism, and assess whether Tocqueville is optimistic or pessimistic about democracy's future.

Joseph Schumpeter (1883–1950), an Austrian-born economist who taught at Harvard, published Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy in 1942. The set reading is Part IV, "Socialism and Democracy", which contains his famous redefinition of democracy.

Critique of the "classical doctrine" (chapter 21)
- The classical doctrine, which Schumpeter associates with eighteenth-century thought, says democracy realises the common good by letting the people decide issues through electing representatives who carry out their will.
- He attacks it on several grounds:
  - There is no uniquely determined common good that all rational people could agree on, because people want different things.
  - Even if people agreed on a goal, they would disagree on how to reach it.
  - The "will of the people" is not a coherent, rational thing. Citizens have a reduced sense of reality about national politics, which is remote from their daily lives. The typical citizen drops to a lower level of mental performance in politics than in their own affairs and is open to manipulation by interests and advertising.
  - Any "will" that emerges is often manufactured by leaders rather than the starting point of the process.

"Another theory of democracy" (chapter 22)
- The democratic method is "that institutional arrangement for arriving at political decisions in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a competitive struggle for the people's vote".
- The people's role is to produce a government (or an intermediate body that produces one) and to remove it. Democracy means only that the people have the opportunity to accept or refuse those who would rule them.
- The theory gives leadership its proper place: political initiative comes from leaders, as in economics it comes from entrepreneurs. Competition for votes is like competition in a market.
- Voters should respect a political division of labour: once they have elected someone, they should not try to direct them ("back-seat driving").
- Advantages Schumpeter claims: a workable criterion to distinguish democracies from other regimes; a realistic account of how democracy works; a link between democracy and individual freedom, since competition for leadership requires some freedom of discussion.

Conditions for success (chapter 23)
- High-quality politicians.
- A limited range of political decision: not everything should be decided politically.
- A well-trained, independent bureaucracy.
- Democratic self-control by politicians and voters, and tolerance of differences of opinion.

Influence and criticism
- Schumpeter's "minimalist" or "elite" theory influenced later economic theories of democracy (e.g. Anthony Downs, An Economic Theory of Democracy, 1957) and much empirical political science.
- Participatory democrats (e.g. Carole Pateman, Participation and Democratic Theory, 1970) argued he had redefined democracy to fit low participation and stripped out its educational value.
- Critics ask whether competition for votes is enough to make a system democratic if citizens have no real say over policy, and whether his low view of citizens is self-fulfilling.

Connections in POL1
- Weber's plebiscitary leadership democracy is an important precursor.
- The Federalist also values representatives over direct popular rule, but on different grounds (refinement rather than realism about citizens).
- Mair's "void" can be read as Schumpeter's model hollowed out: competition persists but voters disengage.

Exam tips: present the critique of the classical doctrine before the definition, quote the definition accurately, and evaluate whether minimalism is a description or a defence of democracy.

The Lent Term lectures on contemporary representative democracy use four texts. They ask whether Western representative democracy is hollowing out, whether it is linked to prosperity, and whether it might come to an end.

Peter Mair, Ruling the Void: The Hollowing Out of Western Democracy (2013)
- Published after Mair's death in 2011. It opens by declaring that the age of party democracy has passed: parties still exist, but they have become so disconnected from society that they no longer seem able to sustain democracy in its present form.
- Two-way withdrawal:
  - Citizens withdraw: falling turnout, declining party membership, weaker party identification and greater electoral volatility.
  - Elites withdraw: parties move from society into the state, relying on state resources and becoming governing agents rather than representatives. This links to the "cartel party" thesis that Mair developed with Richard Katz in 1995.
- Governments are torn between being responsive (to voters) and responsible (to markets, international commitments and long-term considerations). Increasingly they choose responsibility.
- Depoliticisation: decisions move to non-majoritarian bodies such as central banks, courts and the European Union, which Mair saw as a political system designed to be safe from popular democracy.
- The "void" between citizens and elites helps explain the rise of populist challengers who promise to restore popular sovereignty.

Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, Why Nations Fail (2012)
- The main cause of differences in national prosperity is institutions, not geography or culture.
- Inclusive economic institutions (secure property rights, open markets, the rule of law) encourage investment and innovation. Extractive institutions concentrate wealth in a narrow elite.
- Political institutions underpin economic ones: inclusive economic institutions need pluralistic political institutions with enough central authority.
- Illustrations: Nogales, Arizona versus Nogales, Sonora; North versus South Korea.
- Critical junctures (such as the Black Death or the opening of Atlantic trade routes) interact with small institutional differences to set countries on divergent paths; in England this path led to the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and pluralist institutions. Virtuous and vicious circles then reinforce them.
- Extractive institutions can deliver growth for a while (as in the Soviet Union) but not sustained, innovation-led growth.
- Acemoglu and Robinson, with Simon Johnson, received the Nobel memorial prize in economics in 2024 for work on how institutions shape prosperity.
- Critics question how measurable "inclusive" is, and point to cases such as China's rapid growth under authoritarian rule.

Cornelius Castoriadis (1922–1997), A Society Adrift
- A Greek-French thinker and co-founder of the group Socialisme ou Barbarie. Central idea: autonomy, meaning a society that explicitly and lucidly makes its own laws and institutions, as opposed to heteronomy, where institutions are taken as given by gods, nature or history.
- He argued that so-called representative democracies are better described as liberal oligarchies: once citizens elect representatives, they hand over their power. He admired the Athenian model of direct self-government.
- Revolution, in his sense, means a society's explicit self-institution, not simply violent seizure of power.

Dimitris Vardoulakis, Stasis Before the State (2018)
- Develops a theory of agonistic democracy: conflict (the Greek stasis) comes before and underlies the state, rather than being something the state simply suppresses. The set thesis argues that judgement is constitutive of democracy.

Exam tips: use Mair for the empirical case that representative democracy is hollowing out, Acemoglu and Robinson for its link with prosperity, and Castoriadis for a radical critique of representation itself. Connect them back to Schumpeter, Tocqueville and Constant. Check the set chapters for Castoriadis and Vardoulakis against your current paper guide.

notes.h: Marx and Engels, The Communist Manifesto (1848)
notes.body:
Karl Marx (1818–1883) and Friedrich Engels (1820–1895) wrote the Manifesto of the Communist Party for the Communist League. It was published in London in February 1848, just as revolutions broke out across Europe. It is a programmatic pamphlet, not a full statement of Marx's theory.

Opening
- "A spectre is haunting Europe – the spectre of communism."
- "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles" (Engels later added a note excluding prehistoric society).

Section I: Bourgeois and proletarians
- Society is splitting into two great hostile classes, the bourgeoisie (owners of the means of production) and the proletariat (wage labourers who own nothing but their labour power).
- The bourgeoisie has played a "most revolutionary part". It has destroyed feudal ties, replaced them with "naked self-interest" and "callous cash payment", created a world market and unleashed enormous productive forces. Constant change means that "all that is solid melts into air".
- The state: "The executive of the modern state is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie." Political power is the organised power of one class for oppressing another.
- Crises of overproduction show that bourgeois productive forces have outgrown bourgeois property relations.
- Capitalism creates its own "grave-diggers": by concentrating workers in factories it makes them a class conscious of shared interests. The fall of the bourgeoisie and victory of the proletariat are "equally inevitable".

Section II: Proletarians and communists
- Communists have no interests separate from the proletariat as a whole; they represent the movement's international and long-term interests.
- Their theory can be summed up as the abolition of private property, meaning bourgeois property in the means of production, not personal possessions earned by one's own labour.
- They answer objections that communism would abolish freedom, the family, nations and culture, arguing that these are bourgeois forms. "The working men have no country."
- The first step is to raise the proletariat to the position of ruling class, "to win the battle of democracy", and use political supremacy to centralise production in the hands of the state.
- They list measures for advanced countries, including a heavy progressive income tax, abolition of inheritance, centralisation of credit in a state bank, state control of communication and transport, and free education for all children in public schools.
- When class distinctions disappear, public power will lose its political character, and an association will replace class society, in which "the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all". (The phrase "withering away of the state" comes later, from Engels.)

Sections III and IV
- Section III criticises other socialisms (feudal, petty-bourgeois, "true", conservative and utopian).
- Section IV sets out communists' relations with other opposition parties and ends with the call: "Proletarians of all countries, unite!" (often rendered "Workers of the world, unite!").

Key debates
- Is the Manifesto's view of the state purely instrumental (a tool of the ruling class), or does it allow the state some independence?
- Has history refuted the prediction of polarisation and revolution, or does globalisation vindicate the account of capitalism's dynamism?
- What role is there for democracy in the transition?

Exam tips: quote accurately, separate the analysis of capitalism (often admired even by critics) from the political programme, and connect the Manifesto's account of the state to Weber, Hayek and Schmitt.

Mohandas K. Gandhi (1869–1948) wrote Hind Swaraj ("Indian Home Rule") in Gujarati in November 1909, on board the ship Kildonan Castle travelling from London to South Africa. It was serialised in his South African paper Indian Opinion, banned by the British authorities in India, and published by Gandhi in his own English translation in 1910. It takes the form of a dialogue between a "Reader", a young impatient nationalist, and an "Editor" (Gandhi).

The question of swaraj
- Swaraj means self-rule. Gandhi rejects the view of many nationalists that it simply means driving out the British and governing India with the same institutions: that would be "English rule without the Englishman", keeping the tiger's nature while getting rid of the tiger.
- True swaraj is first self-rule in the sense of mastery over oneself. It is a moral and spiritual condition that each person must achieve, which is why the POL1 lecture calls this "the sovereign soul".

How India was lost
- "The English have not taken India; we have given it to them." Indians welcomed the East India Company for commercial gain and kept the British there through their own desire for modern goods, jobs and institutions.

The critique of modern civilisation
- The real enemy is modern civilisation, not the English people. Modern civilisation makes bodily welfare and material comfort the object of life and multiplies wants without limit.
- Gandhi criticises railways (spreading plague and famine and weakening attachment to place), lawyers (who profit from disputes and strengthened British rule) and doctors of modern medicine (who encourage indulgence by curing its consequences).
- He is scornful of the English Parliament, which he presents as wasteful, swayed by party and the press, and incapable of acting well on its own.
- Against this he sets the older civilisation of India, which he presents as teaching self-restraint and duty and showing that happiness is largely a mental condition.

Means and ends: passive resistance
- The Reader argues for violence to expel the British. Gandhi answers that means and ends are inseparable: the means are like a seed and the end like a tree. Violent means produce a violent order.
- Passive resistance (satyagraha, "truth-force" or "soul-force") is opposed to "body-force" or "brute force". It means accepting suffering oneself rather than inflicting it, and requires chastity, poverty, truth and fearlessness. Gandhi thinks it is the strongest force, available to all.
- He also emphasises education in self-control and moral character, the use of Indian languages, and swadeshi (reliance on local production, such as hand-spinning).

Debates
- Is Hind Swaraj a rejection of the modern state altogether, or a call to transform it? Gandhi's stress on swaraj as self-mastery suggests that true self-rule does not depend on capturing or redesigning the state, but readers disagree about how far he rejects the state itself.
- Is the critique of modern civilisation romantic and backward-looking, or a serious challenge to modern assumptions about progress?
- How does its view of politics as moral self-discipline compare with Weber's ethic of responsibility, or with Fanon's defence of violence?

Exam tips: explain the double meaning of swaraj (national independence and self-mastery), use the means–ends argument precisely, and contrast Gandhi with Fanon on violence and with Hobbes on sovereignty.

notes.h: Schmitt, The Concept of the Political (1927/1932)
notes.body:
Carl Schmitt (1888–1985) was a German jurist and political theorist. The Concept of the Political first appeared as an essay in 1927 and was expanded in 1932. Schmitt joined the Nazi Party in 1933 and is a deeply controversial figure, but his critique of liberalism remains influential on both right and left.

The criterion of the political
- "The concept of the state presupposes the concept of the political." The state is defined by politics, not the other way round.
- Each domain of human life has its own distinction: morality (good and evil), aesthetics (beautiful and ugly), economics (profitable and unprofitable). The specifically political distinction is between friend and enemy.
- The enemy is the public enemy (in Latin, hostis, not inimicus), a collectivity that is existentially "other" and opposed to one's way of life. It need not be morally evil or ugly, and no private hatred is required.
- The political is not a separate subject area but the most intense degree of association and dissociation. Any antagonism (religious, economic, ethnic) becomes political when it is intense enough to group people as friends and enemies.
- The friend–enemy grouping includes the real possibility of physical killing. War is not the aim of politics, but the ever-present possibility of war shapes political behaviour.

The state and sovereignty
- The state is the political unit that decides who the enemy is (the jus belli: the right to wage war and dispose of citizens' lives) and maintains internal peace.
- This links to Schmitt's earlier claim in Political Theology (1922) that the sovereign is the one who decides on the exception.
- Pluralist theories (such as those of Harold Laski and G. D. H. Cole), which treat the state as one association among many, cannot explain who decides in a serious conflict.
- A world without the political (without friend–enemy distinctions) would be a world without states. Because the political world is a "pluriverse" of states, a universal state of humanity is impossible.

The critique of liberalism
- Liberalism tries to avoid the political by neutralising and depoliticising conflict. It turns the enemy into an economic competitor or a debating partner, and puts individual rights and private property ahead of the state.
- Liberalism has no political theory of its own, only a critique of politics aimed at limiting the state.
- Wars fought in the name of humanity are especially dangerous: when a state fights in the name of humanity it claims a universal concept against its enemy, denying the enemy the quality of being human and justifying extreme inhumanity. Schmitt writes that whoever invokes humanity wants to cheat.

Debates
- Is the friend–enemy distinction a neutral description or a dangerous glorification of conflict? Critics link it to his Nazi involvement.
- Does it capture something liberal theory misses, namely the persistence of deep conflict and the need for decision?
- Agonistic democratic theorists borrow from Schmitt while trying to turn enemies into adversaries; Vardoulakis's account of stasis can be compared here.

Connections in POL1
- Hobbes: both see the state's purpose as preventing internal conflict and both stress decision, but Schmitt criticised Hobbes for allowing a private sphere of conscience that liberalism later expanded.
- Weber: both define the state through force, but Schmitt grounds it in the friend–enemy distinction.
- Fanon: the colonial world as divided into two hostile camps.

Exam tips: quote the friend–enemy criterion precisely, explain why the enemy is public not private, and evaluate the critique of liberal "neutralisation".

notes.h: Fanon and MacKinnon: the imperial state and the state and women
notes.body:
The last two set texts ask whose state the modern state is. Fanon examines the colonial state and decolonisation; MacKinnon examines the state from the standpoint of women.

Frantz Fanon, The Wretched of the Earth (1961)
- Fanon (1925–1961) was a psychiatrist from Martinique who worked in a hospital in Algeria during the war of independence and joined the Algerian National Liberation Front (FLN). The book appeared in 1961, shortly before his death, with a preface by Jean-Paul Sartre.

"On violence"
- Decolonisation is always violent, because it replaces one "species" of people with another: the last shall be first.
- The colonial world is a world cut in two, a Manichaean world. The settlers' town is well fed and well lit; the native town is hungry and crowded. The colonised are dehumanised.
- The colonial state rules directly through force (the police officer and the soldier), not through the indirect means of the bourgeois state.
- Violence by the colonised against the coloniser is presented as a response to colonial violence and as a means of liberation. At the individual level, Fanon says it frees the colonised from their inferiority complex and restores self-respect; at the collective level, it unites the people.
- Critics accuse Fanon of glorifying violence; defenders read him as diagnosing a violence colonialism had already created. The book also includes psychiatric case studies of the damage done by the colonial war to people on both sides.

"The pitfalls of national consciousness"
- After independence, a weak national bourgeoisie may simply take the colonisers' place, acting as an intermediary for foreign capital and creating a one-party state ruled by a leader.
- Fanon looks instead to the peasantry and to political education of the masses, and calls for a new humanism rather than imitating Europe.

Catharine MacKinnon, Toward a Feminist Theory of the State (1989)
- MacKinnon, an American legal scholar, builds a feminist theory by analogy with and critique of Marxism. In her account, sexuality is to feminism what work is to Marxism: what is most one's own, yet most taken away.
- Gender is a hierarchy of power: male dominance and female subordination, organised around sexuality. It is not simply difference.
- Method: consciousness-raising, in which women collectively describe their experience, is the feminist method of knowing.
- The liberal state claims to be neutral and objective, but MacKinnon argues it adopts the male point of view as its standard. In her words, "the state is male in the feminist sense": the law sees and treats women the way men see and treat women.
- Examples: rape law (built around men's perceptions of consent), pornography (which she argues is a practice of sex discrimination, and against which she drafted civil rights ordinances with Andrea Dworkin in the 1980s), and abortion law (she criticises grounding abortion rights in privacy, because the private sphere is where women are most subordinated).
- Equality: she rejects both the "sameness" and "difference" approaches and proposes a dominance approach, asking whether a practice keeps women subordinate.
- Critics argue that she universalises women's experience, underplays women's agency and threatens free expression.

Connections and contrasts
- Both reject the liberal claim that the state is neutral: for Fanon it is the settler's state, for MacKinnon it is male.
- Both use and modify Marxist analysis (class for Fanon, sex class for MacKinnon).
- They differ on means: Fanon's defence of anti-colonial violence contrasts with MacKinnon's use of law to transform the state.
- Compare Gandhi's non-violence with Fanon, and Hobbes's or Weber's definitions of the state with both critiques.

Exam tips: avoid caricature. Explain the arguments behind Fanon's account of violence and MacKinnon's account of the male state, and test them against the liberal theories in Section A.

cards.b: When the sovereign can no longer protect the subject: obligation lasts as long as the power to protect.

Passion, a sense of responsibility and a sense of proportion (judgement).

Collective, direct exercise of sovereignty (deliberating, voting laws, judging), compatible with subjection of the individual to the community.
The peaceful enjoyment of private independence: rights of opinion, religion, property, association, occupation, and influence on government.

cards.f: Economic control as control of all ends

Labour: biological necessity (animal laborans). Work: fabricating a durable world (homo faber). Action: speech and deeds among plural humans.
The condition of action: we are all human, but no two people are ever the same.
Each birth is a new beginning; humans can begin something new, the basis of action.

cards.b: Promising (against unpredictability) and forgiving (against irreversibility).
Household concerns (economy, welfare) become the central business of public life, replacing action with behaviour and conformity.
The launch of the first artificial satellite (1957), read as a wish to escape the earth and the human condition.
Citizens united by a common passion or interest adverse to others' rights or the permanent and aggregate interests of the community.
Control its effects through a large representative republic: 'extend the sphere' to include more interests.
'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition'; 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.'
Judiciary is the least dangerous branch, with 'neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment'; defends judicial review.
American government is distinguished by the total exclusion of the people in their collective capacity from any share in it.

Federalists: representatives refine and enlarge public views. Brutus: representatives should resemble and share the feelings of constituents.
Equality of conditions.

Individualism: calm withdrawal into a small circle of family and friends. Egoism: passionate love of self.

Voters should not try to direct representatives between elections ('back-seat driving').
Good politicians, limited range of decisions, competent independent bureaucracy, democratic self-control and tolerance.
Pateman (1970): minimalism defines democracy to fit low participation and ignores its educational role.

Governments must respond to voters but also act responsibly towards markets, treaties and long-term needs; responsibility increasingly wins.
