questions.q: Which is NOT one of Hobbes's three principal causes of quarrel in Leviathan, chapter 13?
options: Glory
Religion
Diffidence
Competition
questions.why: Hobbes names competition, diffidence (distrust) and glory. Religious disagreement matters greatly elsewhere in Leviathan, but it is not one of the three causes listed in chapter 13.

questions.q: According to Leviathan, chapter 21, when may a subject lawfully refuse the sovereign's command?
options: When the sovereign has broken the covenant
When a majority of subjects agree to resist
Whenever he judges the command unjust
When commanded to kill or wound himself
questions.why: Hobbes holds that the right to preserve one's life cannot be transferred, so a subject may refuse to kill or wound himself. Private judgement of justice is no ground for disobedience, the sovereign is not a party to the covenant and cannot breach it, and majority resistance has no special authority in his theory.

questions.q: Explain how, in Leviathan, Hobbes gets from the state of nature to an absolute sovereign.
markScheme: State of nature: equality, three causes of quarrel, war of all against all, no justice or property
Right of nature and laws of nature (seek peace; lay down right to all things; keep covenants)
Covenants unreliable without a common power ('without the sword, but words')
Covenant of each with each to authorise a representative; unity of the commonwealth
Authorisation implies sovereign cannot injure subjects; not party to covenant; sovereignty undivided
Limits: inalienable right of self-preservation; obligation lasts while protection lasts
questions.modelAnswer: Hobbes begins with human beings who are roughly equal in ability and so hope for the same things. Competition, diffidence and glory make them enemies, and without a common power they live in a war of every man against every man, where there is no industry, justice or property. Each has the right of nature to do whatever preserves their life, but reason also discovers laws of nature: seek peace, lay down the right to all things if others will, and keep covenants. Covenants cannot be trusted without a power to enforce them, so people covenant each with each to authorise one man or assembly to act for them all. This makes the multitude one person, the commonwealth, with the sovereign as its representative. Because subjects are the authors of the sovereign's acts, the sovereign cannot injure them, cannot be punished by them and is not party to the covenant. Sovereignty must also be undivided, since divided power leads back to civil war. Its only limit is the inalienable right of self-preservation: subjects may resist threats to their lives, and obligation ends when the sovereign can no longer protect them.

questions.q: Which of the following best matches Weber's definition of the modern state?
options: The unity that decides who is friend and who is enemy
The executive committee of the ruling class
An association that pursues the common good of its members
A community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory
questions.why: Weber defines the state by its specific means, the legitimate monopoly of physical force in a territory, rather than by any end such as the common good. The 'executive committee' formula is Marx and Engels' description of the bourgeois state, and the friend–enemy decision is Schmitt's criterion of the political.

questions.q: In 'Politics as a Vocation', how does Weber relate the ethic of conviction and the ethic of responsibility?
options: They are identical once properly understood
The ethic of conviction should always prevail in politics
They are opposed, but in a mature politician they can become complementary
The ethic of responsibility is suitable only for bureaucrats
questions.why: Weber contrasts the two sharply but suggests that a mature person who acts on the ethic of responsibility may reach a point of saying 'Here I stand; I can do no other', where the two complement each other. He warns against politics guided only by conviction, he does not treat them as identical, and he contrasts the politician's personal responsibility with the official's impartial administration.

questions.q: Explain Weber's distinction between the ethic of conviction and the ethic of responsibility, and why he thinks politics poses special ethical problems.
markScheme: Ethic of conviction: act rightly, leave results to God; blame consequences on others/world
Ethic of responsibility: answer for foreseeable consequences
Politics' specific means is violence/force, so good ends may require dubious means
Ethical irrationality of the world: good can produce evil and vice versa
Mature politician combines them ('Here I stand'); passion, responsibility, proportion
questions.modelAnswer: Weber says all ethically oriented action can follow one of two maxims. Under the ethic of conviction, one does what is right and leaves the results to God: if a pure act has bad consequences, the world, other people's stupidity or God's will is to blame. Under the ethic of responsibility, one must answer for the foreseeable consequences of one's actions. Politics poses special problems because its specific means is power backed by violence. Anyone who engages in politics makes a pact with 'diabolical powers', since achieving good ends often requires morally dubious or dangerous means, and good intentions frequently produce bad results: the world is ethically irrational. A politician guided only by conviction, such as the revolutionary syndicalist Weber discusses, can end up producing disaster while disclaiming responsibility. Weber's ideal is a politician with passion for a cause, a sense of responsibility and a sense of proportion, who acts responsibly yet at some point can say with Luther 'Here I stand; I can do no other', so that the two ethics become complementary.

questions.q: Which of these did Constant identify as a reason why ancient liberty was unsuitable for modern states?
options: The growth of slavery
The spread of direct democracy
The replacement of war by commerce
The decline of representative institutions
questions.why: Constant argued that commerce had replaced war as the main way of getting what one wants, giving individuals independence and occupying their time. The others are wrong: he defended representative institutions, the spread of direct democracy was not his claim, and he cited the abolition (not growth) of slavery, which leaves citizens less leisure.

questions.q: What is the main danger of modern liberty, according to Constant's 1819 lecture?
options: That citizens, absorbed in private independence, will surrender their share of political power too easily
That representatives will be too closely controlled by voters
That commerce will make the state too poor to defend itself
That citizens will participate too intensely and oppress minorities
questions.why: Constant warns that private enjoyment may lead citizens to neglect political liberty, which is the guarantee of their individual liberty. Excessive participation was the danger of ancient liberty misapplied; he did not argue that commerce impoverishes the state; and his worry was that representatives would be insufficiently, not excessively, supervised.

questions.q: Distinguish Constant's 'liberty of the ancients' from the 'liberty of the moderns', and explain why he thought both were needed.
markScheme: Ancients: collective, direct sovereignty; individual subject to community
Moderns: peaceful enjoyment of private independence, rights
Reasons for change: size, abolition of slavery, commerce
Danger of imposing ancient liberty (Rousseau, Terror) and danger of neglecting political liberty
Political liberty as guarantee of individual liberty; need to combine; representation must be supervised
questions.modelAnswer: For Constant, ancient liberty meant exercising sovereignty collectively and directly, deliberating in the public square, voting laws and judging magistrates, but it was compatible with the individual's complete subjection to the community in private life. Modern liberty is the peaceful enjoyment of private independence: being subject only to law, with freedom of opinion, religion, property, occupation and association. Modern states are large, slavery is abolished so citizens must work, and commerce has replaced war, so people value private independence more. Trying to impose ancient liberty on moderns, as the followers of Rousseau did, produced the Terror. Yet Constant insists modern liberty is not enough on its own. If citizens are absorbed in private life and leave politics to representatives without watching them, rulers will take their power and their private freedoms too. Political liberty is therefore the guarantee of individual liberty, and it also improves citizens morally, so the two must be combined.

questions.q: According to Hayek, why does central economic planning tend towards coercion?
options: Democracy always prefers free markets
Markets inevitably produce monopolies
There is no agreed ranking of all ends, so planners must impose their own values
Planning requires too few officials
questions.why: Hayek's central argument is that a single plan needs a complete ranking of ends that no society agrees on, so values must be imposed. The claim that markets inevitably create monopolies is a socialist argument he rejects, he does not claim democracy always prefers markets, and he thinks planning requires extensive discretionary power rather than too few officials.

questions.q: Which statement about Hayek's position in The Road to Serfdom is accurate?
options: He defends democracy as valuable in itself whatever its results
He rejects all state regulation of working conditions
He argues that planning is compatible with the rule of law
He accepts that a minimum of food, shelter and clothing can be guaranteed to all
questions.why: Hayek explicitly allows a guaranteed minimum and some regulation, which is why he is not a pure laissez-faire thinker. He accepts some regulation of working conditions, he treats democracy mainly as a means of safeguarding liberty, and his chapter on the rule of law argues that planning is incompatible with it.

questions.q: Explain Hayek's argument that economic planning is incompatible with the rule of law.
markScheme: Definition: government bound by fixed, general rules announced beforehand
Rule of law lets individuals foresee state coercion and plan their own affairs
Planning requires discretionary decisions about particular people and circumstances
Formal equality before the law conflicts with pursuit of substantive (distributive) goals
Consequence: arbitrary power; possible objection or evaluation
questions.modelAnswer: For Hayek the rule of law means that government in all its actions is bound by rules fixed and announced beforehand. These rules should be general and abstract, like the rules of the road, so that individuals can foresee how the state will use its coercive power and plan their own lives within them. Central planning works differently. To direct production towards particular ends, planners must make detailed decisions about who gets what, which firms expand and which close. These depend on circumstances that cannot be foreseen and on judgements about the relative importance of different people's needs. Planning therefore needs discretion rather than general rules. Pursuing a particular distribution also means treating different people differently, which conflicts with formal equality before the law. As planning extends, legislation becomes a grant of unlimited powers to authorities, and arbitrary power replaces the rule of law. Critics reply that modern regulatory states combine substantial economic intervention with legal constraints, so the incompatibility may be a matter of degree.

questions.q: In The Human Condition, which activity corresponds to the human condition of plurality?
options: Contemplation
Action
Work
Labour
questions.why: Arendt ties action to plurality, because it goes on directly between distinct people through speech and deeds. Labour corresponds to life itself (biological necessity), work to worldliness (making a durable world), and contemplation belongs to the vita contemplativa, not the three activities of the vita activa.

questions.q: According to Arendt, what are the remedies for the unpredictability and irreversibility of action?
options: Labour and work
Planning and punishment
Sovereignty and law
Promising and forgiving
questions.why: Arendt finds the remedies within action itself: promising creates islands of predictability, and forgiving releases people from irreversible deeds. Planning and sovereignty belong to the model of making (or of mastery) that she criticises as a substitute for action; she does discuss punishment, but as an alternative to forgiving, and planning is no remedy at all. Labour and work are different activities altogether.

questions.q: Explain Arendt's distinction between labour, work and action, and why she thinks the modern world threatens action.
markScheme: Labour: biological process, consumption, endless; animal laborans
Work: fabrication of durable world; means–end; homo faber
Action: speech and deeds among plural equals; natality; disclosure of who one is
Modern threat: rise of the social, victory of animal laborans, society of jobholders, behaviour replacing action
Nuclear/space-age theme: acting into nature, world/earth alienation
questions.modelAnswer: Labour is the activity that corresponds to the biological life of the body: producing food and other necessities that are consumed almost immediately, in an endless cycle. Work is the fabrication of durable objects that together make a stable human world; homo faber works according to a model and uses means to achieve ends. Action is the only activity that goes on directly between people: through speech and deeds they reveal who they are, begin something new (natality) and generate power when acting together. It depends on plurality and on a public space where people appear to one another. Arendt thinks modernity threatens action. The rise of 'the social' makes economic life and welfare the central business of politics, so that behaviour and conformity replace action. Labour triumphs, and we become a society of jobholders. Meanwhile, scientists 'act into nature' with nuclear and space technologies, starting processes nobody can control, while citizens lose a shared public world.

questions.q: In Federalist 10, what does Madison identify as the most common and durable source of factions?
options: Differences of religion
Attachment to different leaders
The unequal distribution of property
Regional differences between states
questions.why: Madison lists religion, attachment to leaders and other sources, but says the most common and durable source has been the various and unequal distribution of property. Regional differences between states are not singled out as the main cause in Federalist 10.

questions.q: Which argument is made by Brutus rather than by Publius?
options: Extending the sphere makes majority faction less likely
A free republic cannot exist over a territory as large as the United States
Ambition must be made to counteract ambition
The judiciary is the least dangerous branch
questions.why: Brutus, drawing on Montesquieu, argued that a free republic could not cover so large a territory. The other three are Publius: Federalist 51 on ambition, Federalist 78 on the judiciary, and Federalist 10 on extending the sphere.

questions.q: How does Madison argue in Federalist 10 that a large republic is better able than a small one to control the effects of faction?
markScheme: Definition of faction; causes sown in human nature; property
Removing causes would destroy liberty; so control effects
Pure democracy cannot check majority faction
Republic: representation refines and enlarges public views; more fit characters chosen in large districts
Extending the sphere multiplies interests, making an oppressive majority harder to form and coordinate
Evaluation (e.g. Brutus's counter-argument, elitism)
questions.modelAnswer: Madison defines a faction as a group, majority or minority, united by a passion or interest adverse to the rights of others or the permanent interests of the community. Its causes are sown in human nature, above all in the unequal distribution of property. Removing them would destroy liberty or require impossible uniformity of opinion, so the only remedy is to control faction's effects. A minority faction can be defeated by majority vote, but a majority faction is dangerous. A pure democracy offers no cure, because a majority can easily act together to oppress others. A republic, governed through representatives, can do better. Representatives may refine and enlarge public views, and in a large republic each represents more citizens, so there is a wider choice of fit characters and it is harder to win by corrupt means. Above all, extending the sphere brings in a greater variety of parties and interests, making it less likely that a majority will share a motive to oppress others, or be able to coordinate if they do. Brutus replied that such a distant, small body of representatives would not resemble or be accountable to the people.

questions.q: What does Tocqueville identify as the 'generating fact' of American democracy?
options: Federalism
The separation of church and state
Universal male suffrage
Equality of conditions
questions.why: Tocqueville says equality of conditions is the fact from which all others derive. Federalism, the separation of church and state and the extent of the suffrage are institutions he discusses, but he treats them as consequences or supports of the social state of equality.

questions.q: How does Tocqueville distinguish individualism from egoism?
options: Individualism is a virtue; egoism is a vice
Individualism belongs to aristocracies; egoism to democracies
Individualism is a calm, considered withdrawal into a small circle; egoism is a passionate love of self
They are the same, but individualism is the newer word
questions.why: Tocqueville describes individualism as a reflective, peaceful feeling that leads citizens to withdraw from society, while egoism is an instinctive, passionate self-love. He treats individualism as a danger, not a virtue; he links it specifically to democratic equality rather than aristocracy; and he insists the two are distinct.

questions.q: What does Tocqueville mean by 'soft despotism', and what features of American society did he think could guard against it?
markScheme: Immense tutelary power providing for welfare and pleasures; keeps citizens in perpetual childhood
Arises from equality, individualism and love of material well-being
Degrades rather than tyrannises; relieves citizens of thinking and acting for themselves
Remedies: associations, local self-government, free press, jury
Religion, self-interest properly understood, mores
questions.modelAnswer: In the second volume Tocqueville imagines a new kind of despotism suited to democratic times. Equal, isolated individuals, each withdrawn into private life and preoccupied with petty pleasures, live under an immense tutelary power that takes charge of their security, needs and pleasures. Like a parent, it seeks to keep them in perpetual childhood. It does not torment or destroy but softens, regulates and gradually relieves citizens of the trouble of thinking and acting for themselves, while they console themselves that they chose their guardians. Against this, Tocqueville points to the habits of American freedom. Local self-government, especially in the New England township, draws citizens into public affairs. Civil and political associations teach the art of combining. A free press and the jury educate citizens in judgement. Religion moderates materialism, and self-interest properly understood links private interest to public good. Ultimately he relies on mores: active, self-governing habits of heart and mind.

questions.q: According to Schumpeter, what is the essential role of the people in a democracy?
options: To express a coherent general will
To produce a government and to remove it
To instruct representatives between elections
To decide policy issues directly
questions.why: Schumpeter's minimalist account limits the people to producing (and dismissing) governments through competitive elections. Deciding issues and expressing a general will belong to the classical doctrine he rejects, and he explicitly criticises voters directing representatives between elections ('back-seat driving').

questions.q: Which of the following is one of Schumpeter's criticisms of the 'classical doctrine' of democracy?
options: It exaggerates the role of political leaders
Elections are too infrequent
There is no uniquely determined common good on which all rational people could agree
Representatives are too responsive to voters
questions.why: Schumpeter argues that no common good exists that all could agree on through rational argument. He does not complain that representatives are too responsive or that elections are too infrequent, and he argues the reverse of the claim about leaders: the classical doctrine ignores leadership, which his alternative theory puts at the centre.

questions.q: Set out Schumpeter's 'other theory of democracy' and assess one objection to it.
markScheme: Definition: institutional arrangement where individuals acquire power to decide by competitive struggle for the people's vote
People produce and remove governments; leadership and initiative; market analogy
Political division of labour; no back-seat driving
Conditions for success (quality of politicians, limited scope, bureaucracy, self-control/tolerance)
Objection (e.g. Pateman: participation; or emptiness of choice) with assessment
questions.modelAnswer: Schumpeter defines the democratic method as the institutional arrangement in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a competitive struggle for the people's vote. The people's role is to produce a government and to dismiss it, so democracy means only that they can accept or refuse those who would rule them. Leaders take the initiative, rather like entrepreneurs competing for customers, and once elected they should be left to govern without voters 'back-seat driving'. The method works best when politicians are of high quality, the range of political decisions is limited, an expert bureaucracy exists, and voters and politicians show democratic self-control and tolerance. Participatory democrats such as Pateman object that this definition simply ratifies low participation and loses democracy's educational value: citizens become passive because the system gives them nothing to do. This objection has force, because Schumpeter's low view of citizens may be self-fulfilling. But Schumpeter could reply that his theory describes how large democracies actually work and still distinguishes them clearly from dictatorship.

questions.q: According to Acemoglu and Robinson, what mainly explains the different prosperity of Nogales, Arizona and Nogales, Sonora?
options: Ignorance of good policies by Mexican leaders
Their different geography and climate
Their different cultures
Their different institutions
questions.why: The two halves share geography, climate and much culture, so Acemoglu and Robinson use them to show that institutions, not geography, culture or ignorance, explain the difference.

questions.q: Which pair best captures Peter Mair's account in Ruling the Void?
options: Parties gain members while turnout rises
Citizens become more partisan while parties become more representative
The EU becomes more democratic while national parties decline
Citizens withdraw from party politics while party elites withdraw into the state
questions.why: Mair describes a mutual withdrawal: citizens disengage (lower turnout, membership and loyalty) and party elites retreat into government and the state. Rising partisanship, more representative parties, growing membership and higher turnout all reverse his findings, and he saw the EU as designed to be insulated from popular democracy rather than becoming more democratic.

questions.q: What does Peter Mair mean by the 'hollowing out' of Western democracy, and how does it relate to Schumpeter's theory?
markScheme: Age of party democracy has passed; parties disconnected from society
Citizens' withdrawal: turnout, membership, identification, volatility
Elites' withdrawal into state; cartel party; responsive vs responsible government
Depoliticisation: delegation to non-majoritarian bodies (central banks, courts, EU); populism
Relation to Schumpeter: competition remains but meaningful choice/engagement shrinks
questions.modelAnswer: Mair argues that the age of party democracy has passed: parties still compete, but they have become so disconnected from society that they no longer sustain democracy as before. Citizens are withdrawing, with lower turnout, falling party membership, weaker party identification and more volatile voting. Party elites are also withdrawing, moving from society into the state, relying on state resources and acting as governors rather than representatives (linked to the 'cartel party' thesis). Governments increasingly choose to be 'responsible' to markets, treaties and expert bodies rather than 'responsive' to voters, and decisions are delegated to central banks, courts and the EU. This leaves a void between rulers and ruled that populists exploit. Mair's picture can be read as Schumpeter's model taken to an extreme. Competition for votes continues, but voters increasingly lack real choices or connection, so even the thin link that Schumpeter relied on, the ability to accept or refuse rulers, loses meaning.

questions.q: In The Communist Manifesto, the modern state's executive is described as:
options: A neutral arbiter between classes
The realisation of the general will
A temporary alliance of workers and peasants
A committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie
questions.why: Marx and Engels call the executive of the modern state 'but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie'. They reject the idea that the state is a neutral arbiter or the embodiment of a general will (a Rousseauian notion), and a worker–peasant alliance is not their description of the modern state.

questions.q: What do Marx and Engels mean by the 'abolition of private property' in the Manifesto?
options: Confiscation of all personal possessions
Abolition of bourgeois property in the means of production
Return to feudal common land
Abolition of all taxation
questions.why: They specify that communism does not deprive anyone of the power to appropriate products of society; it abolishes bourgeois property, the private ownership of the means of production used to exploit others' labour. They explicitly deny aiming to take away personal possessions earned by one's own labour, they propose a heavy progressive income tax rather than abolishing taxes, and they do not seek a return to feudal forms.

questions.q: Why do Marx and Engels describe the bourgeoisie as having played 'a most revolutionary part' in history, and why do they think it creates its own 'grave-diggers'?
markScheme: Destroyed feudal, patriarchal relations; 'naked self-interest', 'callous cash payment'
Constantly revolutionises production; 'all that is solid melts into air'; world market; huge productive forces
Crises of overproduction: productive forces outgrow property relations
Creates proletariat, concentrated in factories; becomes class-conscious and organised
Fall of bourgeoisie and victory of proletariat 'equally inevitable'
questions.modelAnswer: Marx and Engels credit the bourgeoisie with transforming the world. It destroyed feudal, patriarchal and religious bonds and replaced them with 'naked self-interest' and 'callous cash payment'. It cannot exist without constantly revolutionising the instruments and relations of production, so that 'all that is solid melts into air'. It created a world market, drew all nations into civilisation and unleashed productive forces greater than all previous generations together. But these forces outgrow bourgeois property relations, as shown in recurring crises of overproduction. The bourgeoisie also creates the class that will overthrow it. Capitalism produces a proletariat of wage labourers who own nothing but their labour power. By concentrating them in factories and cities and linking them through modern communications, it turns isolated workers into an organised, class-conscious movement. In this sense the bourgeoisie produces its own grave-diggers, and its fall and the proletariat's victory are, they claim, equally inevitable.

questions.q: In Hind Swaraj, what does Gandhi mean by criticising 'English rule without the Englishman'?
options: Expelling the British but keeping their institutions and civilisation would not be true swaraj
India needs a parliament on the English model
India should be ruled by Englishmen who adopt Indian customs
British rule is acceptable if Indians hold the offices
questions.why: Gandhi argues that expelling the British while keeping modern Western institutions would be keeping the 'tiger's nature' without the tiger, not true self-rule. He does not want Englishmen to rule in Indian dress, he does not accept continued British rule with Indian office-holders, and he is scornful of the English Parliament.

questions.q: Which best describes Gandhi's argument about means and ends in Hind Swaraj?
options: Means and ends are inseparable: the means are like a seed and the end like a tree
The end matters more than the means
Violence is acceptable as a last resort against tyranny
Any means are justified if the end is independence
questions.why: Gandhi rejects the Reader's view that violent means are justified by the goal of independence, arguing that means shape ends as a seed shapes a tree. He does not endorse violence as a last resort, and he insists that ends do not outrank means.

questions.q: Explain why Gandhi treats modern civilisation, rather than the British, as India's real enemy in Hind Swaraj.
markScheme: 'The English have not taken India; we have given it to them': Indians' own desire for gain sustained rule
Modern civilisation makes bodily welfare and material comfort the object of life; multiplies wants
Examples: railways, lawyers, doctors; Parliament
Swaraj as self-rule/self-mastery, not just expelling the British
Implication: remedy is moral reform, swadeshi, passive resistance
questions.modelAnswer: Gandhi argues that India was not conquered by force but given away: Indians welcomed the East India Company for profit and continue to sustain British rule through their own desire for modern goods, jobs, courts and education. The British are thus less the cause than a symptom. The deeper cause is modern civilisation, which makes bodily welfare and material comfort the purpose of life, multiplies wants without limit and treats people as means to production. He illustrates this with railways, which spread disease and weaken ties to place, lawyers who profit from quarrels and helped entrench British rule, and modern doctors who encourage indulgence. He is also contemptuous of the English Parliament. Because the problem is a civilisation that Indians themselves have adopted, simply removing the English would leave 'English rule without the Englishman'. True swaraj requires self-rule in the sense of self-mastery: Indians must reject modern civilisation's values, practise swadeshi and use passive resistance, so that independence follows from moral transformation.

questions.q: What is Schmitt's criterion of the political?
options: The distinction between public and private
The distinction between good and evil
The distinction between friend and enemy
The distinction between rulers and ruled
questions.why: Schmitt argues that the specifically political distinction is between friend and enemy. Good and evil is the moral distinction, which he insists is separate; public and private is Arendt's central distinction, not his criterion; and rulers versus ruled is not the criterion he proposes.

questions.q: Why does Schmitt think liberalism fails to grasp the political?
options: It tries to neutralise conflict, turning enemies into economic competitors or debating partners
It overemphasises war and the enemy
It denies the existence of individual rights
It concentrates too much power in the sovereign
questions.why: Schmitt argues that liberalism depoliticises conflict, dissolving the enemy into a competitor in the market or an opponent in discussion. He does not accuse it of over-concentrating sovereign power (it limits the state), of emphasising war, or of denying individual rights, which it puts first.

questions.q: Explain Schmitt's friend–enemy distinction and why he thinks the political is a matter of intensity rather than a separate domain.
markScheme: Political distinction is friend/enemy, parallel to good/evil, beautiful/ugly, profitable/unprofitable
Enemy is public (hostis), existentially other; no private hatred or moral evil needed
Real possibility of physical killing / war as presupposition
Any antagonism (religious, economic, ethnic) becomes political when intense enough
State as the unit deciding on the enemy (jus belli); 'state presupposes the political'
questions.modelAnswer: Schmitt argues that each sphere of human activity rests on a basic distinction: good and evil in morality, beautiful and ugly in aesthetics, profitable and unprofitable in economics. The specifically political distinction is between friend and enemy. The enemy is a public enemy (hostis), a collectivity that threatens one's way of life and could, in the extreme case, be fought; it need not be evil or ugly, and no private hatred is required. The real possibility of physical killing is what gives the distinction its meaning, although war is not the aim of politics. Because the friend–enemy grouping marks the utmost degree of association and dissociation, the political has no subject matter of its own. Any opposition, whether religious, economic, moral or ethnic, becomes political once it is intense enough to divide people into friends and enemies. The political unit, normally the state, is the entity that decides on this grouping in the decisive case; hence 'the concept of the state presupposes the concept of the political'.

questions.q: According to Fanon in The Wretched of the Earth, the colonial world is:
options: A Manichaean world cut in two, ruled directly by force
A liberal order governed by consent
A world in which the colonised and settlers share a public sphere
A unified society moving gradually towards equality
questions.why: Fanon describes a compartmentalised, Manichaean world divided between settler and native towns and ruled by the police officer and soldier. He rejects the idea that colonialism is gradually becoming equal, liberal or based on consent, and stresses the absence of any shared public space.

questions.q: What does MacKinnon mean when she says 'the state is male in the feminist sense'?
options: Most legislators and judges are men
The law sees and treats women the way men see and treat women, while claiming neutrality
Biological differences make men better suited to rule
The state should be run by women
questions.why: MacKinnon's claim is about the state's point of view: its supposed neutrality and objectivity embody the male standpoint. The point is not simply that office-holders are male, she does not argue that women should run the state, and she rejects biological explanations of gender hierarchy.

questions.q: Compare how Fanon and MacKinnon challenge the claim that the modern state is neutral.
markScheme: Fanon: colonial state rules by direct force; Manichaean, compartmentalised world; settler's state
Fanon: decolonisation and violence; pitfalls of national bourgeoisie reproducing domination
MacKinnon: state adopts male point of view; liberal neutrality/objectivity as male standard
MacKinnon: examples (rape, pornography, privacy/abortion); dominance approach; consciousness-raising
Comparison: both adapt Marxist structural analysis; differ on means (violence vs law)
Evaluation / link to liberal theorists (Hobbes, Weber, Constant)
questions.modelAnswer: Both reject the liberal picture of the state as an impartial umpire. For Fanon, the colonial state is the settlers' state. It divides the world into a well-fed settler town and a crowded native town and rules the colonised directly through police and soldiers rather than through consent. Its violence dehumanises the colonised, which is why Fanon presents decolonisation as necessarily violent and liberating. He also warns that, after independence, a national bourgeoisie may simply take over the same state and continue domination. For MacKinnon, the liberal state's neutrality is the male point of view presented as objectivity: the law sees and treats women as men see and treat them. Rape law built around men's perceptions, the failure to treat pornography as discrimination, and grounding abortion in privacy all show how formally neutral law protects male dominance. Both use structural analysis adapted from Marxism, colonial domination for Fanon and sex class for MacKinnon. They differ sharply on remedies: Fanon defends anti-colonial violence, whereas MacKinnon seeks to transform the state through law. Together they challenge Section A's theorists, such as Weber's account of legitimacy and Constant's account of liberty, to ask whose state and whose liberty these are.

questions.q: 'Hobbes's sovereign protects subjects from each other, but leaves them defenceless against the sovereign.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains why Hobbes thinks absolute, undivided sovereignty is needed (state of nature, unreliable covenants, divided sovereignty → civil war)
Explains authorisation: subjects as authors; sovereign cannot injure them; not party to covenant; cannot be punished
Identifies protections that remain: right of self-preservation (ch. 21), silence of the law, obligation tied to protection
Considers sovereign's duties under the laws of nature and the interest of the sovereign in subjects' prosperity
Considers objections (Locke-style: 'polecats and lions'; no institutional checks)
Hobbes's reply: comparison with the state of nature; any check would need a higher power
Uses textual evidence accurately (chapters 13, 17, 18, 21, 29)
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement captures a real tension in Leviathan, but it overstates Hobbes's vulnerability. Hobbes's case for an absolute sovereign begins in chapter 13. Rough equality, competition, diffidence and glory produce a war of every man against every man, and covenants without a common power are 'but words'. Peace requires that each covenant with each to authorise one man or assembly as their representative. Because subjects are authors of everything the sovereign does, the sovereign cannot injure them; because he is not party to the covenant, he cannot breach it; and he cannot be lawfully punished (chapter 18). Sovereignty must be undivided, since divided power, as in England, leads to civil war (chapter 29). In this sense there are no institutional defences against the sovereign: no right of rebellion, separation of powers or court above him.

But subjects are not wholly defenceless. Chapter 21 preserves rights that cannot be transferred: a subject may resist those who come to kill, wound or imprison him, need not accuse himself, and may refuse dangerous commands such as killing himself. Obligation lasts only as long as the sovereign can protect, so a sovereign who cannot protect loses his claim. Subjects also enjoy the liberty of the 'silence of the law', and the sovereign is bound in conscience by the laws of nature, including equity, even if subjects cannot enforce them. Hobbes adds a prudential argument: the sovereign's strength depends on his subjects' prosperity, so he has little interest in harming them.

Critics can answer with Locke's image (aimed at absolute monarchy in the Second Treatise) that it is foolish to guard against polecats and foxes only to be devoured by lions. Natural-law duties without enforcement may be empty, and an individual's right to resist offers little defence against a determined state. Hobbes's reply is comparative: any check on the sovereign would need a higher power to enforce it, recreating the problem, and the worst sovereign is better than civil war.

I conclude that Hobbes does leave subjects without political or legal defences against the sovereign, deliberately. He does not leave them without any protection: their inalienable right of self-preservation, and the conditional nature of obligation, mark limits that make his theory less absolute than the statement suggests.

questions.q: 'Representative democracy was designed to keep the people out of government.' Discuss with reference to The Federalist and at least one other set text.
markScheme: Interprets the claim: representation as exclusion versus as a form of popular rule
Federalist 10: refining and enlarging public views; extended republic; control of majority faction
Federalist 63: 'total exclusion of the people in their collective capacity'; Senate's role; Federalist 51 checks
Brutus: representatives should resemble the people; too few, elite; consolidation
Second text used well (e.g. Constant's supervised stewards; Schumpeter's minimalism; Mair's void; Castoriadis' liberal oligarchy; Tocqueville's local participation)
Distinguishes exclusion from direct rule from exclusion from all influence (elections, accountability)
Considers whether exclusion is a defect or a protection (minorities, rights, competence)
Reasoned conclusion with accurate references
questions.modelAnswer:
There is strong textual support for the claim. In Federalist 10 Madison defends a republic, meaning government by representation, as superior to pure democracy precisely because it does not let the people decide directly. Representatives will 'refine and enlarge the public views', and an extended republic makes it harder for a majority faction to form and act. Federalist 63 identifies what distinguishes American government from ancient democracies as the total exclusion of the people in their collective capacity from any share in government. The Senate, indirect election of the President, life-tenured judges with power of judicial review (Federalist 78), and checks and balances (Federalist 51) all slow down and filter popular majorities. Brutus saw this clearly: with so few representatives over so vast a territory, government would fall to the wealthy and distant, who would not resemble or understand ordinary people.

Yet 'keeping the people out' needs qualifying. Publius excludes the people from governing directly, not from power altogether. The House is elected frequently by the people, and the whole system rests on popular consent; Madison's aim is to protect minorities and rights from majority faction, not to establish aristocracy. Constant offers a similar but more balanced defence: modern citizens, busy with private life, delegate to representatives as the rich hire stewards, but they must supervise them, because political liberty guarantees their private freedom.

Schumpeter makes the exclusionary reading explicit and embraces it. Democracy is only a competitive struggle for the people's vote; the people produce and remove governments and should not 'back-seat drive'. Critics such as Castoriadis call such regimes liberal oligarchies, and Mair's account of citizens and elites withdrawing from each other suggests that what was designed as a filter has become a void.

I conclude that representative democracy was designed to keep the people out of the direct exercise of power, and that its founders saw this as a feature, not a flaw. But it was also designed to make government depend on popular consent and removability. Whether this counts as 'democratic' depends on whether we accept the Federalists' and Schumpeter's view of popular rule or the more demanding standards of Brutus and Castoriadis.
